claims.claim: The Books and Boots essay argues that Martin's vocabulary systematically excludes almost all words derived from Latin, Greek or French.
claims.source: Simon, Books & Boots blog, 'George RR Martin's prose style - Affixes, compound and combination words' (2013)
claims.quote: systematic exclusion from his vocabulary of almost all words

claims.claim: The Books and Boots essay asserts that Martin's style shows a high frequency of words of Anglo-Saxon origin.
claims.quote: his style shows a high frequency of words of Anglo-Saxon origin

claims.claim: The Books and Boots essay reports that the common Latin and Greek prefixes it lists are almost never found in Martin's work.
claims.quote: Almost none of these are found in Martin

claims.claim: The Books and Boots essay argues that Martin reserves his rare neoclassical words for scenes whose speaker or setting is legalistic or learned, naming the maesters and the septons' court as the places they appear.
claims.quote: deploying them carefully to distinguish scenes where he wants to accentuate
claims.page: GRRM's practice, 3. use of combining forms

claims.claim: The Books and Boots essay identifies the archaic native prefix a- in atop, abed and ahorse as a deliberate archaism in Martin's prose.
claims.quote: he conspicuously deploys the archaic prefix

claims.claim: The Books and Boots essay concludes that the scarcity of Latin, Greek and French sourced words is what makes Martin's prose feel archaic.
claims.quote: The result is to make his prose feel archaic

claims.claim: Blatt's corpus for the book includes eight George R. R. Martin novels, the appendix listing Dying of the Light, Fevre Dream, The Armageddon Rag and the five published Song of Ice and Fire volumes.
claims.source: Ben Blatt, Nabokov's Favorite Word Is Mauve (2017), appendix of books used, pages 240-241
claims.quote: George R. R. Martin—8 Novels Dying of the Light Fevre Dream

claims.claim: Blatt's cinnamon-words table gives Martin the three words dragons, cloaks and unsullied as the words he uses most anomalously often.
claims.source: Ben Blatt, Nabokov's Favorite Word Is Mauve (2017), cinnamon words and nod words table, page 175
claims.page: p. 175, table of cinnamon words and nod words

claims.claim: Blatt states that the tables of clichés and favourite words in his book cover the fifty authors he has been using as examples throughout it.
claims.source: Ben Blatt, Nabokov's Favorite Word Is Mauve (2017), page 172
claims.quote: fifty authors I've been using as examples throughout this book

claims.claim: Blatt reports that for every 10,000 words E L James writes, 155 are -ly adverbs, against 134 for Meyer and an average of 105 for King.
claims.source: Ben Blatt, Nabokov's Favorite Word Is Mauve (2017), chapter 1 'Use Sparingly', page 13
claims.quote: 155 are -ly adverbs . For Meyer the count is 134

claims.claim: Blatt's 'Use Sparingly' chapter prints its per-book adverb tables for Hemingway and Steinbeck, and a full-text search of the volume returns Martin's name on no page of that chapter.
claims.source: Ben Blatt, Nabokov's Favorite Word Is Mauve (2017), chapter 1 'Use Sparingly', pages 9-27
claims.quote: Adverbs per 10,000 Words - Steinbeck The Winter of Our Discontent

claims.claim: The A Song of Ice and Fire Wiki's chapter table for A Game of Thrones totals 292,332 words.
claims.source: A Song of Ice and Fire Wiki, 'A Game of Thrones/Statistical Analysis'

claims.claim: The same wiki table counts 73 point-of-view chapters shared among nine characters in A Game of Thrones.
claims.source: A Song of Ice and Fire Wiki, 'A Game of Thrones/Statistical Analysis'

claims.claim: The wiki gives Eddard Stark 15 of the book's chapters and 53,467 words, 18.29% of the novel.
claims.source: A Song of Ice and Fire Wiki, 'A Game of Thrones/Statistical Analysis'
claims.page: Unique POV Breakdown table, Eddard Stark row

claims.claim: The wiki's chapter-by-chapter table for A Game of Thrones gives its shortest chapter 1,696 words and its longest 7,334 words.
claims.source: A Song of Ice and Fire Wiki, 'A Game of Thrones/Statistical Analysis'
claims.page: Chapter by Chapter Breakdown, chapters 17 and 34
